steps.label: Asymmetric Encryption
steps.content:
2.3 Encryption

Asymmetric Encryption

Year 10

  • Today: how two different keys fix the weak point of symmetric encryption.
  • You already know: plain text, cipher text, the key, and symmetric encryption with one shared key.
Think → Pair → ShareLast lesson ended on a weak point of symmetric encryption. What was it, and why does it matter?Show the answer

The key has to be shared. If it is intercepted on the way, whoever has it can decrypt every message.

steps.label: The Problem: People Who Have Never Met
steps.content:
The Problem: People Who Have Never Met

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ana buys from a shop in another country. She has never met anyone there. How can they agree a symmetric key that Eve never sees? Why is that hard?Show the worked answer

They cannot meet in person, so the key must be sent across the network.

Anything sent can be intercepted. If Eve gets the key, she can decrypt everything.

  • Symmetric: the same key encrypts and decrypts, so the receiver must be sent the key.
  • We send data to shops, banks and websites we have never met.
  • Any key sent across a network can be intercepted.
  • Today's question: can we encrypt with a key that is safe to send?
Ana→key ?→Shop
Eve intercepts everything sent
No safe way to send the key

steps.label: A Padlock Anyone Can Close
steps.content:
A Padlock Anyone Can Close

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ben posts open padlocks to anyone who asks. He keeps the only key. Ana locks a box for Ben with one. Eve has a padlock too. Can Eve open the box? Why?Show the worked answer

No. A padlock closes without a key, but only Ben's key opens it.

Having a padlock lets Eve lock boxes, not open them.

  • Anyone can close an open padlock. Closing needs no secret.
  • Only the key opens it, and Ben never sends his key.
  • So it does not matter who sees the padlock on the way.
  • Next: the same idea with two encryption keys.
Ben→open padlock→Ana
Eve sees the padlock: no problem
Ana locks the box→locked box→Ben opens it with his key
Eve sees the locked box: cannot open it

steps.label: Asymmetric Encryption: Public Key and Private Key
steps.content:
Asymmetric Encryption: Public Key and Private Key

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Ben sends his public key to Ana. Eve copies it on the way. Can Eve decrypt Ana's message to Ben? Why?Show the worked answer

No. The public key only encrypts. It cannot decrypt.

Decrypting needs Ben's private key, and that never left Ben's computer.

  • Asymmetric encryption uses two different keys: a public key and a private key.
  • Ben makes both keys. They work together.
  • The public key encrypts. Ben gives it to anyone, even Eve.
  • The private key decrypts. Ben keeps it. It is never sent.
  • Data encrypted with Ben's public key can only be decrypted with Ben's private key.
Ben→Ben's public key→Ana
plain text→Ben's public key→cipher text
cipher text→Ben's private key→plain text
Eve has the public key and the cipher text: meaningless

steps.label: Compare: Eve Intercepts the Key
steps.content:
Compare: Eve Intercepts the Key

Think → Pair → ShareBoth times, Eve intercepts the key that is sent and then the cipher text. Predict: in which case can she read the message? Why?Show the answer

Left: the key that was sent also decrypts, so Eve reads the message.

Right: the key that was sent only encrypts. The key that decrypts was never sent.

Symmetric

Ana sends Ben the shared key.
Eve intercepts: the key + cipher text
The same key decrypts.

Eve reads it

Asymmetric

Ben sends Ana his public key.
Eve intercepts: public key + cipher text
The public key cannot decrypt.

Meaningless to Eve

  • Eve intercepted everything that was sent, both times.
  • Asymmetric never sends the key that decrypts.

steps.label: Compare: Ben's Public Key and Chen's Public Key
steps.content:
Compare: Ben's Public Key and Chen's Public Key

Think → Pair → ShareAna writes to Ben. The first time she encrypts with Ben's public key. The second time she uses Chen's public key by mistake. Predict: can Ben read each one? Why?Show the answer

First: yes. Ben's private key matches Ben's public key.

Second: no. Only Chen's private key can decrypt it, and only Chen has that.

Encrypted with Ben's public key

Sent to Ben.
Ben uses Ben's private key.
The keys match.

Ben reads it

Encrypted with Chen's public key

Sent to Ben.
Ben uses Ben's private key.
The keys do not match.

Meaningless to Ben

  • Everyone has their own public key and private key.
  • Encrypt with the public key of the person who will read the message.

steps.label: Compare: Symmetric and Asymmetric
steps.content:
Compare: Symmetric and Asymmetric

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Eve can intercept every message, including any key that is sent. Which method still keeps the data safe? Why?Show the answer

Asymmetric. The only key it sends is the public key, and that cannot decrypt.

Symmetric must send the key that decrypts, so Eve could get it.

SymmetricAsymmetric
KeysOne shared keyTwo keys: a public key and a private key
Encrypt withThe shared keyThe receiver's public key
Decrypt withThe same keyThe receiver's private key: a different key
Is the key that decrypts sent?Yes: it must reach the receiverNo: it is never sent
  • The same in both: a key is used, plain text becomes cipher text, intercepted data is meaningless.
  • Asymmetric is more secure: there is no key exchange to intercept.

steps.label: Exam Question: Two Differences
steps.content:
Exam Question: Two Differences

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a good difference name both methods in one sentence?Show the answer

The mark is for the contrast. Say what one method does, then "whereas", then what the other does instead.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/13, November 2024, Question 2(g)(iii). The email data is encrypted using asymmetric encryption before it is sent.

items.prompt: (iii) Give two differences between symmetric encryption and asymmetric encryption.
items.modelAnswer: Any two from: symmetric uses one key, whereas asymmetric uses two keys (public and private); symmetric can send the key with the data, whereas asymmetric does not; symmetric decrypts with the same key, whereas asymmetric decrypts with a different key; symmetric is less secure than asymmetric.

Cambridge IGCSE 0478/12, March 2024, Question 7(a)(ii). Data is transmitted using the internet. The data is encrypted before transmission.

items.prompt: (ii) Describe the differences between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
items.modelAnswer: Four from: symmetric has a shared key ... to encrypt and decrypt; both the sender and receiver know the key; asymmetric has different keys, a public key and a private key; ... the public key encrypts the data and the private key decrypts it; anyone can know the public key, but only those intended know the private key.
